domain_assessment.role: County emergency-management Training Officer controlling a full-scale exercise and transitioning to a real incident response
domain_assessment.objective: Identify and respond to an unexpected real-world winter-weather incident while safely suspending the exercise, coordinating shelter operations, allocating constrained transportation resources, and handing command to the Incident Commander
domain_assessment.incident_type: A real fast-moving winter storm and communications/tower failure occurring during a scripted shelter-in-place and evacuation exercise

decision_points.summary: Pause the exercise and verify whether ambiguous reports and a weather alert reflected a real incident rather than a scripted inject.
evidence_before: A live weather alert describing a faster-moving winter storm
Two field reports that the participant could not immediately classify as scripted or real
The inject timing and content did not match the exercise script
evidence_after: Actual weather data confirmed a real tower failure
Roads were closing faster than forecast
The exercise was paused rather than allowed to continue into a live emergency
goals_constraints: Avoid feeding exercise scenario content into an active real incident
Accept a small loss of exercise time if verification proves unnecessary
alternatives: Continue the drill and treat the reports as scripted
Pause the drill and verify against live data
decision_points.decision_basis: The participant noticed a mismatch between the known inject list and the incoming reports, then sought disconfirming or clarifying real-world evidence before acting.
decision_points.time_pressure: Moderate; the participant faced an emerging weather event but described verification as costing only a few minutes.
decision_points.uncertainty: High initially because the reports could plausibly have been either exercise material or real operational information.

decision_points.summary: Brief two newly rotated liaison officers at the shelter using familiar facility-specific shorthand rather than checking their knowledge or conducting a fuller orientation.
evidence_before: Two liaison officers arrived for a scheduled shift handoff
Neither had worked at that specific shelter before
The participant had approximately twenty-five minutes before needing to address transportation
The participant did not ask about either officer's prior familiarity with the shelter layout, current muster point, or local terminology
evidence_after: A group was sent to the old west muster point
A volunteer coordinator asked what 'Zone C protocol' referred to
The participant later recognized that a map walk-through would probably have exposed the obsolete muster point
goals_constraints: Transfer shelter-operational knowledge to incoming liaisons
Maintain continuity during the emerging incident
Use available time before transportation decisions became necessary
alternatives: Give the customary abbreviated verbal rundown using local shorthand
Ask about site familiarity and current muster-point knowledge
Walk through the current zone map and shelter layout from first principles
Provide a written or visual briefing aid
decision_points.decision_basis: The participant treated internally familiar terms as if they were self-explanatory operational names and assumed that liaison officers would generally acquire the relevant conventions quickly.
decision_points.time_pressure: Low to moderate. The text explicitly establishes approximately twenty-five minutes with no immediate transportation task, although some time was voluntarily spent double-checking transportation numbers.
decision_points.uncertainty: Resolvable but unexamined. The participant knew the officers were new to the site yet did not test whether they shared the required facility-specific knowledge.

decision_points.summary: Prioritize transportation to the sector whose roads were closing fastest rather than distributing two buses evenly among three requesting sites.
evidence_before: Two buses were available for three sites requesting transport
Fuel and driver-hour limits constrained operations
County updates indicated that one sector's roads were closing faster than the others
evidence_after: The prioritized site cleared before becoming inaccessible
Another site waited longer but received transport after the first run
goals_constraints: Avoid stranding people at a site that was about to become unreachable
Allocate scarce buses under fuel and driver-hour limits
Accept unequal waiting times where necessary to reduce access risk
alternatives: Split buses evenly across all three sites
decision_points.decision_basis: The participant prioritized asymmetric closure risk over superficially equal distribution, judging that equal allocation could leave one site inaccessible.
decision_points.time_pressure: Moderate to high because road closures were progressing.
decision_points.uncertainty: Moderate; road-closure timing and transport consequences were dynamic, but the county updates supplied decision-relevant evidence.

decision_points.summary: Fully suspend the exercise and provide the Incident Commander with a written status briefing rather than informally running exercise debriefing and real command in parallel.
evidence_before: The Incident Commander arrived to take over the real incident
Exercise evaluators still expected a formal debrief
Shelter operations were partly proceeding under the earlier liaison arrangement
evidence_after: The Incident Commander received a written status briefing
The handoff created a checkable record rather than relying only on verbal memory
goals_constraints: Transfer accurate incident status under time pressure
Prevent exercise administration from competing with real command
Reduce loss of details in degraded communications conditions
alternatives: Run the exercise debrief and real command informally in parallel
Suspend the exercise and conduct a formal written handoff
decision_points.decision_basis: The participant preferred a written artifact because it could be checked against operational conditions and reduced reliance on recalled verbal information.
decision_points.time_pressure: Moderate to high because command transfer and active shelter operations were concurrent.
decision_points.uncertainty: Moderate; the participant needed to preserve an accurate, shared operational picture despite communication degradation.

target_occurrence_audit.supporting_quote: “I didn't ask about their broader background — I assumed liaison officers generally pick up our zone conventions fast” and “Those terms are just how I refer to things day to day — they don't register as shorthand to me, they register as the actual names.”
target_occurrence_audit.evidence_location: Decision-point-2 briefing sequence: the participant's explanation of the liaison handoff, the probe about the available twenty-five minutes, and the follow-up probe concerning what the officers already knew.
target_occurrence_audit.mechanism: The participant's own well-established facility-specific knowledge changed content selection and calibration during the handoff. Familiar shorthand was experienced as self-explanatory rather than as tacit local knowledge requiring translation. Despite knowing that the incoming officers were new to that shelter and despite having available time, the participant neither assessed their knowledge nor supplied the missing context. The later confusion about Zone C and the obsolete muster point corroborates the knowledge gap, though the participant's stated cognitive framing—not the bad outcome alone—is the primary evidence.
target_occurrence_audit.plausible_nonbias_explanation: A routine, standardized handoff protocol or an organizational expectation that all liaison officers are prequalified on site conventions could otherwise explain the abbreviated briefing. The interview weakens that alternative because the participant explicitly says the officers were new to the site, had time to ask or orient them, and did not perceive the familiar terms as shorthand requiring explanation.
target_occurrence_audit.additional_evidence_needed: None for classification. A minor optional enhancement would be a concrete example of what the participant believed “Zone C protocol” entailed before learning that the liaisons lacked that shared meaning, but the present evidence is sufficient.

revision.location: Decision point 2, especially the answers beginning “I knew they were new to this shelter specifically” and “Honestly, it didn't occur to me that it needed to be longer.”
revision.current_defect: No material defect. The episode contains a discrete briefing decision, an observable knowledge-assumption mechanism, a missed knowledge check, and a downstream indication that the recipient did not share the assumed context.
preserve: The two liaison officers' lack of prior experience at the specific shelter
The approximately twenty-five-minute available briefing window
The participant's use of “usual Zone C protocol” and “standard muster point”
The participant's statement that the terms felt like actual names rather than shorthand
The later Zone C confusion and old-muster-point misdirection
avoid_creating: Do not add an explicit bias label or textbook explanation
Do not add an independent heuristic-based, authority-based, or time-pressure-based failure at another decision point
Do not recast the failure as caused by lack of time, because that would undermine the counterfactual isolation

additional_candidate_biases.bias: Status quo bias or habitual-response reliance
additional_candidate_biases.supporting_quote: “With the liaisons, I gave them the same rundown I always give” and “Having the extra time didn't change how I framed it.”
additional_candidate_biases.mechanism: The participant repeated a familiar briefing routine despite a situational cue that the officers were new to the site and despite the removal of acute time pressure.
additional_candidate_biases.plausible_nonbias_explanation: The repeated routine is better explained by the supported curse-of-knowledge mechanism: the participant did not perceive familiar terminology as compressed or incomplete. The text does not establish a preference for the existing routine because of inertia, loss aversion, or a perceived cost of changing it.

additional_candidate_biases.supporting_quote: “A bit, in hindsight. I think I was more deliberate about not leaving room for gaps after seeing what happened with the liaison briefing.”
additional_candidate_biases.mechanism: The participant retrospectively connects the earlier briefing failure to a more careful written handoff.
additional_candidate_biases.plausible_nonbias_explanation: This is ordinary learning from immediate feedback and an adaptive change in error-control strategy. The participant does not claim that the earlier outcome had been predictable or obvious before it occurred.

nonbias_cues.cue: The participant relies on prior exercise experience to recognize that the reports do not fit the inject script.
nonbias_cues.why_not_bias: This is justified expertise followed by active verification against live weather data. The participant does not merely trust intuition or dismiss conflicting evidence.

nonbias_cues.cue: The participant pauses the exercise despite losing drill time.
nonbias_cues.why_not_bias: The decision is a proportionate risk-management response to ambiguous operational information. The participant explicitly weighs the downside of a short delay against the possibility of missing a real emergency.

nonbias_cues.cue: The participant allocates buses unequally rather than evenly.
nonbias_cues.why_not_bias: Unequal allocation is not evidence of unfairness, outcome bias, or a fairness heuristic. It is based on a stated, decision-relevant difference in road-closure risk and constrained resources.

nonbias_cues.cue: One site experiences a longer wait after the transportation choice.
nonbias_cues.why_not_bias: An unfavorable or uneven outcome does not establish biased reasoning. The available evidence indicates that the choice prevented the more serious risk of an entire site becoming unreachable.

nonbias_cues.cue: The written handoff is influenced by the earlier liaison mix-up.
nonbias_cues.why_not_bias: This is a reasonable response to newly observed communication vulnerability, not hindsight bias. The participant does not retroactively claim foreknowledge of the failure.

nonbias_cues.cue: The participant did not ask about the liaisons' site familiarity.
nonbias_cues.why_not_bias: The omission alone would be an ordinary briefing error. It is classified as curse of knowledge only because the participant supplies a specific mechanism: tacit local terminology was not recognized as shorthand, and role title was treated as implying shared local knowledge.

causal_claims.claim: The liaison briefing failure was not caused solely by insufficient time.
causal_claims.textual_basis: The participant reports having approximately twenty-five minutes before transportation required attention, acknowledges having time to ask directly about site familiarity, and says the expanded briefing did not occur because it did not register as needing expansion.
causal_claims.assessment: Supported at a moderate-to-strong level within the interview.

causal_claims.claim: Assuming shared local knowledge caused under-explanation during the handoff.
causal_claims.textual_basis: The participant explicitly states that liaison officers were assumed to pick up zone conventions, that familiar terms did not register as shorthand, and that no knowledge check occurred. Subsequent Zone C confusion and use of the old muster point are consistent with the proposed pathway.
causal_claims.assessment: Supported. The downstream confusion corroborates the account but should not be treated as sole proof of the bias.

causal_claims.claim: A fuller, map-based briefing would probably have prevented the muster-point error.
causal_claims.textual_basis: The participant says it “probably would have caught the muster point issue immediately.”
causal_claims.assessment: Plausible but counterfactual and not directly demonstrated. It should be phrased as a likely preventative mechanism, not as a certain causal conclusion.

causal_claims.claim: Written handoff reduces detail loss relative to verbal handoff under degraded communications.
causal_claims.textual_basis: The participant states that written material gives the Incident Commander something to check against rather than relying on remembered verbal information.
causal_claims.assessment: Reasonable operational rationale; the interview does not independently test comparative effectiveness.

correlation_causation_risks.risk: Treating the later old-muster-point misdirection as conclusive evidence that curse of knowledge caused the briefing failure.
correlation_causation_risks.mitigation: The classification should rest principally on the participant's documented assumption of shared knowledge and failure to recognize shorthand as compressed local knowledge. The outcome is corroboration only.

correlation_causation_risks.risk: Attributing the liaison failure entirely to available time or entirely to the participant's knowledge assumption.
correlation_causation_risks.mitigation: The counterfactual interview provides evidence against acute time pressure as the primary explanation, but it cannot eliminate all organizational or procedural contributors, such as absent standardized orientation materials.

correlation_causation_risks.risk: Treating the participant's hindsight statement as proof that the earlier failure was foreseeable.
correlation_causation_risks.mitigation: The statement reflects post-event learning and should not be used to infer pre-event predictability.

causal_audit.changed_variable: Amount of time available for the shift-handoff briefing before the next competing transportation task
held_constant: Storm timeline and severity are presented as unchanged within the scenario.
The liaison officers remain newly assigned to the specific shelter.
The same local shorthand is used: “Zone C protocol” and “standard muster point.”
The downstream confusion concerns the same kinds of knowledge gaps: meaning of Zone C and the current muster point.
Transportation resource constraints and the closure-risk prioritization logic remain separate from the liaison briefing episode.
The pause-and-verify decision and the written Incident Commander handoff remain substantively independent of the manipulated briefing-time condition.
causal_audit.explanation: The interview implements the intended causal test effectively: more available briefing time is made salient, and the participant explicitly denies that the brief handoff was an intentional time-saving abbreviation. Instead, the participant explains that familiar terms were not perceived as shorthand and that role-based assumptions substituted for checking recipient knowledge. One minor limitation is that the participant voluntarily spends some of the available period double-checking transportation numbers, but the account still establishes that no immediate competing task forced the abbreviated briefing and that the participant had time to ask the relevant questions.

global_revision_constraints: Retain exactly one Curse of Knowledge occurrence at the liaison handoff.
Preserve the distinction between a knowledge-calibration failure and a time-pressure explanation.
Do not promote the routine-briefing language into a separate status quo or habitual-response bias occurrence.
Do not treat the justified verification, transportation prioritization, written handoff, or post-event learning as target-bias manifestations.
